title: Build binary search
mini_lecture: Binary search works on a sorted array by repeatedly cutting the search space in half. Compare the target to the middle element — if it's smaller, search left; if larger, search right. This gives O(log n) time.
hint: The function definition comes first. Then you need to set up your boundaries before the loop starts.

course: COMP 110 — Introduction to Algorithms and Programming
title: Trace the loop
mini_lecture: A for loop repeats code a set number of times. The range(n) function gives numbers from 0 to n-1. To trace a loop, go step by step — write down what each variable is after every pass through the loop.
hint: Start with total = 0. Each iteration, total gets the current value of i added to it. What is i each time?

content.question: What is total after each iteration?

explanation: Each iteration adds i to total. So: 0+1=1, 1+2=3, 3+3=6, 6+4=10, 10+5=15. This is the sum of numbers 1 through 5. The pattern is called a triangular number — the formula is n(n+1)/2, so 5(6)/2 = 15.

title: Match the Big O
mini_lecture: Big O notation describes how an algorithm's runtime grows as input size increases. O(1) is constant time — it doesn't matter how big the input is. O(log n) means the work halves each step. O(n) is linear. O(n log n) is common for efficient sorts. O(n²) means nested loops over the input.
hint: Think about what each algorithm does. Does it use nested loops? Does it divide the input in half? Does it look at every element once?

content.instruction: Match each algorithm to its correct time complexity

explanation: Binary search halves the input each step → O(log n). Bubble sort and selection sort both use nested loops over the array → O(n²). Merge sort divides the array and merges — divide and conquer → O(n log n). Hash table lookup goes directly to the right slot → O(1) average case.

title: Trace the recursion
teaser: Can you follow the call stack?
mini_lecture: Recursive functions call themselves with smaller inputs until they hit a base case. To trace recursion, follow each call forward until you reach the base case, then work backwards collecting the return values. This is like unwinding a stack of nested boxes.
hint: Start with fib(0) and fib(1) — those are your base cases. Then fib(2) = fib(1) + fib(0). Build up from there.

content.question: What does fib(n) return for each value?

explanation: fib(0)=0 and fib(1)=1 are the base cases. Then fib(2)=fib(1)+fib(0)=1+0=1. fib(3)=fib(2)+fib(1)=1+1=2. fib(4)=fib(3)+fib(2)=2+1=3. fib(5)=fib(4)+fib(3)=3+2=5. This is the Fibonacci sequence. Notice how many redundant calls happen — this is why memoization matters in interviews.

course: COMP 182 — Data Structures and Program Design
title: Build stack push
mini_lecture: A stack follows Last-In-First-Out (LIFO) — think of a stack of plates. Push adds an element to the top. Before pushing, we check if the stack is full. If not, we increment the top pointer and place the item there.
hint: You need to check for overflow first. If it's not full, increment top, then place the item.

content.instruction: Arrange these lines to complete a working push method

explanation: First define the method, then check if the stack is full. If it is, print an error and return early. If there's room, increment top to point to the next empty slot, then place the item there. The order matters — if you placed the item before incrementing, you'd overwrite the current top element.

course: COMP 256 — Discrete Structures for Computer Science
title: Boolean logic
mini_lecture: Boolean algebra uses AND, OR, and NOT to combine true/false values. AND returns true only when both inputs are true. OR returns true when at least one input is true. NOT flips the value. These are the building blocks of every if-statement you'll ever write.
hint: Work from the inside out. First evaluate what's inside the parentheses, then apply NOT, then AND, then OR.

content.question:
What does this expression evaluate to?

(True AND False) OR (NOT False)

explanation: Work inside out. (True AND False) = False. (NOT False) = True. Then False OR True = True. Remember: AND needs both to be true, OR only needs one, and NOT flips the value.

course: COMP 322 — Operating Systems and System Architecture
title: Process scheduling
mini_lecture: In Shortest Job First (SJF) scheduling, the CPU always picks the process with the shortest burst time next. If multiple processes arrive at the same time, the one with the shortest burst goes first. This minimizes average waiting time but requires knowing burst times in advance.
hint: All processes arrive at time 0. Sort them by burst time shortest first, then run them in that order. Track when each one finishes.

content.code:
Process  Burst Time
P1       6
P2       2
P3       8
P4       1

All arrive at time 0
Using Shortest Job First (SJF)
content.question: What time does each process finish executing?

explanation: SJF runs the shortest burst first. P4 (burst 1) runs first, finishes at time 1. P2 (burst 2) runs next, finishes at 1+2=3. P1 (burst 6) finishes at 3+6=9. P3 (burst 8) finishes at 9+8=17. Total waiting time is 0+1+3+9=13, average = 3.25.

title: Pick the right structure
mini_lecture: Choosing the right data structure is one of the most important skills in programming. Each structure has strengths — arrays are great for indexed access, hash maps for fast lookups, stacks for undo operations, queues for ordering tasks, and trees for hierarchical data.
hint: Think about what operation each scenario needs most. Fast lookup? Ordered processing? Undo capability?

content.instruction: Match each scenario to the best data structure
algorithms: Looking up a word in a dictionary
Processing customer support tickets in order

explanation: Undo/redo follows Last-In-First-Out — that's a stack. Dictionary lookup needs fast key-based access — hash map. Support tickets are first-come-first-served — queue. File systems have folders inside folders — tree structure. Index-based access is what arrays do best.
